utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I understand you will be recalling a witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We are dealing with the witness currently under direct examination for Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then you will be calling, who is it, Mrs. Vlacina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. She will be recalled after this witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Mr. Wladimiroff, would you like to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I call again Mr. Dasic. MR. TOMISLAV DASIC, recalled. Examined by MR. WLADIMIROFF, continued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Dasic, you understand that you are still under oath, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Mr. Dasic, when we stopped yesterday you were talking about the ownership of houses by companies, for example, such as the Omarska iron ore mine and apartments owned by the municipality of Prijedor. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do. I remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right. You explained to us that these kinds of companies and communities have their own houses and they use these houses for their employees or civil servants, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would it make any difference for your committee doing your inspections when you inspected a house that belonged to such a community or such a company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my situation I did not have a chance to deal with such flats. The houses were not owned by the municipality; they were privately owned. There were farms, farmhouses, vacated by the Muslims and even some Serbian houses were also vacated, and they were recorded or not recorded as the case might have been for new settlement. In my domain where I was working with my commission, there were no apartments, no flats of the kind that you are describing and we did not record those.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you also told us that the commission functioned in a period of 1st October up to 1st or 15th December 1992, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That you sometimes worked for the whole day, even on Saturdays, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that and that was the way it was; much depending on the weather and also on my free time. Many things which I did not manage to do on Monday or Tuesday, I would work and do on Saturday to make up for what I lost in the beginning of the week and because the job had to be completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You also told us that all three of you did the work together, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we were always together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: At what time would you usually start to work in the morning, or was that not in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since Kozarac is some 18 kilometres away and the region where we were recording the situation is about 18 kilometres from Prijedor, so we would be leaving Prijedor around 8 o'clock, half past 9, even half past 9 and 10.00. Since it was already late autumn, before 8 o'clock in the morning it was very cold, and we did not start before 8 o'clock ever. Sometimes we would be starting from Prijedor at 8.00 or before 8.00, but we were in there on the spot by half past 8 or 9 o'clock so that we could actually start working. We would be already in front of a house which was either vacated and empty or settled by somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Until what time would you continue to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually, as far as I remember, we would be working for three to four hours, about 3 or 4 o'clock, sorry, so we would be ending our daily work around 1500, 1600 hours. We tried to put in six to seven hours of good, solid work every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In that time you also lived in Prijedor, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I lived in Prijedor all the time. I lived there and I spent the nights at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you know where Dusko Tadic lived in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time he also lived in Prijedor and lived there and spent the nights there because he would be returning, he would be going to work with me, go to Kozarac. But he did not stay in Kozarac; he returned with me to Prijedor in the same car and actually we lived in the same district of the city. That was a new settlement of Pecani. The same driver that drove us would be leaving us, dropping us off, in front of our apartments and that the distance was about 300 to 400 metres between the two apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: While you were driving around doing your job for this commission, would you talk about politics with Dusko Tadic or would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we probably did talk politics as well. At that time these were topical events.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did Dusko Tadic express extreme nationalistic sentiments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never noticed that. I never felt that he was an extreme nationalist. We were simply trying to think coolly about the developments and events and I, in fact, liked that. I liked somebody who was moderate, who was not extremist in any way and who was not overheated, so to speak. But, as I told you, I had not known him before. So as we talked, we got to know each better. I liked when I worked with somebody to know who the person is, what his thoughts are and so on. Although Dusko, in fact, had every reason to be more extremist, but in the way he lived, where he lived, did not affect him and he was very fair, I would say correct in his attitudes and was very honest, although he had been exposed to a real tragic development.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yourself, Mr. Dasic, were you politically involved? Were you a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yourself, Mr. Dasic, were you a member of a political party in those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not my language. I do not understand. There might be something wrong with the -- there is a confusion with the languages now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I understand that you do not understand French!

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What I was asking you, Mr. Dasic, is were you involved in politics in those days? Were you a member of a political party in those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I was not involved in politics and I was not a member of any political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Dusko Tadic have a car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember. I do not think he did. I do not think he did, because he would have been using it when we actually badly needed a car and could not get one, but I cannot tell you precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right. That is all I ask, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dasic, you just indicated that at the time in, I guess, the autumn of 1992 you were not a member of any political party. Were you a member of any political party before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was. For 28 years I was a member of the Communist Party, Tito's Party. For 28 years I was a member of that Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated that you became the director of the Prijedor agricultural service as soon as the war began. Was there a director of the service before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I actually was appointed about a month before the outbreak of the war. Before that there had been other directors, both Croats and Serbs, but we never had a Muslim in the position of a director in the agricultural station or agricultural applied service, because this was half an institute, half an experimental farm. We were in charge of promoting and advancing, improving agricultural service. So this was an extension service in agriculture. We worked with hybrid, development of new hybrids, vegetables, fruits, cattle and stock raising. That was our job and we were a specialised service to help the local farmers. Unlike the Institute who would be working not with the farmers but rather with state-owned farms, big farms, we were working with individual private farmers, helping them conducting their work. We organised seminars for them in the winter, in the spring, sowing service. We had various specialists for different parts of agriculture and that was our main activity. We also, as I said already, had our own experimental farm to test and develop new species and new varieties of corn, of maize, wheat. We had pilot farms for milk cows and fattening of calves. So these were the main activities of our agriculture station. Before that, we were part of the Banja Luka Institute. This was a big agricultural estate covering some 26 municipalities. I hope that that explains what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The question was actually whether or not there was a director before you. Let me ask you, who was the director whom you replaced? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Milan Pribicevic, a Serb like myself, so there was no change of nationality in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yesterday you indicated that you were aware of the takeover in Prijedor and you were also asked about the outbreak of the conflict in Kozarac. I believe you indicated that the alleged killing of a soldier who was in a JNA uniform in Jakupovici was one of the direct causes which led to disagreement between the Serbs and Muslims. This disagreement between the Serbs and the Muslims that was caused or triggered by the incident with the soldier, this was the attack on Kozarac, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the -- well, that was about a month and a half later, after the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that something was in the air, something was wrong. The situation was tense, there was uncertainty, and we who were, who knew the situation a little bit better, who followed the events, we knew that something will act as a spark, and that spark was the killing of that soldier. That was on the way to Kozarac at some kind of division line between the Serbian and Muslim, Muslim communities. That was between Banja Luka and Prijedor, Jakupovici. That, as far as I know, was, in fact, one event that triggered the attack - the conflicts between the Serbs and the Muslims. Who attacked whom, whether Muslims attacked the Serbs, Serbs the Muslims, I honestly do not know because I was not there at that time and I could not -- this was not part of my job. I was not that much interested. What I was mainly concerned with was actually simply doing my work and I felt a bit under pressure as a person living in the area. In my view, this was just one sparkle, but the whole thing was hanging in the air and, in fact, it does not matter who started and who killed whom, this was just one case because living in Prijedor we learned that the situation became more and more tense, that the tank was attacked, that a soldier was killed, a local boy. Now, that was what happened. But that was not the day that Kozarac was attacked. Kozarac was attacked, Kozarac was actually attacked two days later on Friday, that was on Friday. Then we had Saturday and actually on Sunday the fighting between Muslims and Serbs broke out between Kozarac and Omarska in that part of the line, along the line dividing the Muslim and Serbian villages. Was that clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By the time you were working in the area as part of the commission, the area of Kozarac had been, essentially, entirely cleansed of the Muslim community, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not quite, not quite at that time. There was still some Muslims but not in Kozarac itself but, rather, in some villages towards Trnopolje. That was according to my information and according to my knowledge from the field. This was not 100 per cent cleansed. The cadastral municipality of Kozarac was not fully cleansed at that time. We are talking now about in September, October, November, there were still some Muslim people living in the cadastral municipality of Kozarac because Kozarac, as a cadastral municipality, is much larger, while the town itself of Kozarac had no Muslims left in Kozarac itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You have explained to us much of the structure and work of the agricultural station. How many people worked for you as director of the agricultural service? How many people were you responsible for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was responsible for 12 people altogether. At the moment I have seven people only because our scope of activities was somewhat reduced during the wartime, but also I have people who work seasonally because we have our own production, we have the experimental farm. So, in fact, we need to take more workers when the season is in full swing. This is now an intermunicipal service. We have more engineers, Masters of science and so on. But the station never had more than 12 to 13 people permanently employed. It never had more. At the moment we have only seven. I was responsible for -- the largest number that I was responsible for was 12 people during my rule, if I may put it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understood that you were, from what you testified yesterday, extremely busy even before your appointment as director. I presume those responsibilities and duties only increased after your appointment as director?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would say, I do work a great deal and I work hard. At the same time, I am also a professional collaborator. I am a court expert. I have my own farm also. So I was working on several fronts and never had much time. When, of course, I became the director, that was just another obligation, and in the state of war it was all the more difficult, so that when I had to leave in the morning, I had to do many of the things in my office, my regular routine work, and then I left for the field. I was not very enthusiastic about being on that commission, but that was a necessity. There was nobody else to do that. Also, I had been living in this part. I knew all the villages and I knew Muslims, Croats and Serbs in the area between Kozarac and Grmec, and I knew how to approach them, how to talk to them. I never had any difficulty contacting people and establishing good relations with them to complete the kind of work which I started to do. I had no prejudice and I was doing my best. I approached everybody openly, frankly, working in my domain. I never touched upon matters which do not concern me. I only deal with professional matters and that was all. So that, as a man, as a human being, I never tried to be superficial in my approach to work. I invested all of my energies into my duties and I could come to any farmer, to any house owner. I could look him in the eye and do my job fairly and I never ha problems with people -- at least not until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the essential task of the commission was to go through the areas you spoke of and determine whether or not any of the homes or habitations were still livable, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the principal task of the commission. That was our assignment, to establish how many houses were still habitable so as to accommodate, so as to house, the refugees; whether they met conditions, that is, whether the water supply was all right, electricity, whether these houses were furbished, if somebody had already moved in, then to establish who had moved in, how many members of the family. We had also cadastral data, who was the owner, the area or plots of land, and those were our principal tasks, or if a person had moved in, why had he done so. I never went into who was supposed to get a particular house. We were simply to go out, make a record, take stock of this, write down the protocol, turn it over to the central commission and that would be that. Of course, sign the protocol, all three members of the commission, but that was that. As I have said, we issued no decisions, no ordinances nor thing. We never issued any decisions, I mean, valid decisions that somebody would be entitled to use a particular house for half a year or for a year or something. Ours was simply to go out into the field, take stock of the situation, make a record of this and then submit it to the central commission. That was our principal assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were part, therefore, of this process of going to private residences and determining whether they were habitable and then providing that information to the authorities of Republika Srpska so that it could be proclaimed as State property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not really get your question. I did not understand well your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. The farms and homes which you surveyed were privately owned, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, privately owned, yes. Yes. They were all private property.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK. Those were homes in the area of Kozarac, Kamicani, Kozarusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were houses in that area, and they -- those were Muslims mostly. They were mostly Muslim houses, that is, houses abandoned by their Muslim owners and they were treated as abandoned, as vacated houses but with private owners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Many of the homes in that area were no longer habitable. They had been destroyed during the conflict, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some which were destroyed and some of them were looted. Of course, in combat operations quite a number of them were destroyed, shall we say, about 40 per cent were not habitable, which did not meet criteria, either because they had been destroyed or looted, plundered or set fire to. But sometimes owners (and there were such instances), when the owner was leaving the house who thought he had to leave the house, he would put it on fire himself, so that there is no some general law, I mean, applicable to all situations and say, "This was so and so and so and so". No, there were all sorts of things and sometimes owners simply torched their own houses themselves. I mean, if his mind was set to go, then rather than leave it to somebody else, he would simply put it on fire. There were such cases. But it was 60 per cent of the houses were habitable, of those houses which we surveyed and during my time on the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you happen to be on the main street of Kozarac during the time you were conducting your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did I happen -- what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you in central Kozarac and on the main street, Marsala Tita, at some point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I used to pass those streets. That was the High Street in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you notice that Dusko Tadic's home had written on it, "Serbian house, do not touch"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was such an inscription, yes, "Serb house, do not touch" on some houses, but there were no people in them. We went into those houses. We did survey them. There would be no one in them, but they did have this graffiti, "Serb house, do not touch", and we would go in and then make a record of what was there and turn it over to the municipal commission. I mean, a person or the owner might have written that and left, and some people also appropriated the right and appropriated two or three houses, that is, misappropriated the right and appropriated two or three houses prior to this commission, because there was a general disarray. There were no authorities, no real power. It was wartime so that it was -- so that some people simply tried to profit from the situation. You know what I mean? When an atomic bomb drops and it is a mess all over. It is very difficult really for one to decide what is the wisest thing to do, and it is very easy to have -- to be clever, to be wise after the event. We were simply caught there unawares. Complete and overall chaos reigned there and even people who were known to be very poised persons panicked at the time because we -- nobody, nobody thought that after 50 years of normal life we would again come to experience this. There were very few people remembering that vast, long time ago. Most of us lived normally; only those who were preparing all this and preparing the ground for all this knew about this. All the rest of us were shocked by it. It was a very difficult moment for us. It was very difficult to decide what to do, while women, children, what to do with them. Some people said one thing, other people said some other thing. It was really difficult to know what was the best to do or what was one supposed to do, how to go about all these things. Some people may say that they did know what would happen, but I did not know. Had I known it, I would have slept well, but as it was, I did not know about this so that I was really caught unawares and very many -- and there were too many things in all, too many things vague, too many moot points, moot questions, something that one could not read even -- find in books and for normal people it was a shock. I really could not wish it on anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the time you were examining these private homes and determining which were habitable, they were still privately owned and still the property of their rightful owners? Once you determined that a home was habitable, you provided that information to the authorities of Republika Srpska, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these were houses which the municipality took for temporary use. It proclaimed them its property, and it was allocated to people not for ever, but only for use for three, six or 12 months -- at least at the time when I was part of the process. We would go out, make a, take stock of the situation, then turn over, turn over this to the commission and then they granted leases or permits for three, six or 12 months, but nobody got such houses for permanent use. I mean, nobody could come and say: "I have left another municipality and another house somewhere, so I am taking up this house". No, no permanent ownership rights. You could get a house for use for three, six or 12 months and you had to sign the protocol saying that you have taken up this house and when you were going out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know how much compensation was provided to the Muslim owners when their property was appropriated by Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No compensation was paid, as far as I know, neither in cash nor in property, nor anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You have indicated that at the time there were people who needed residences; there were more people who needed residences than there were residences available. Was there a priority system developed for who would receive those homes, flats or apartments which were available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is something that was not within my province. This is the central commission of the municipality which they did. They had some criteria. They had a set of priorities on the basis of which they ruled. I really do not know what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But you are ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess the number of children, how many members in a family. I would not really know, but it would be my guess that that was one of the conditions, one of the priorities, I would say. Although, of course, sometimes, as we are want to do, sometimes we give to somebody who is least needy and those who are more in need are not given something. Those are those who go outside priorities, but otherwise ----

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were aware that service during the war, during the conflict, was one of the priorities or one of the factors that gave a person a priority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is rather likely, yes, I guess they would have some priority there. There must have been instances of that kind, or a child who is closer to his mother, of course, will be breast fed before the child who is further away from his mother. So I think that some were given the houses even though they were not really entitled to on the basis of some other priorities. Some may have been given a bigger house or given a house sooner simply because they were closer to authorities. I mean, these things do happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is all I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Just one question, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have just one question. Mr. Dasic, you told us yesterday that your commission covered the area of the cadastral municipality of Kozarac. You explained that your commission WAS working in Kozarac, a part of Trnopolje called Hrnici, Kozarusa, Kamicani and a part of Dera and a part of Bozici, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That was the area covered by my commission, except that we did not finish all the work because the weather changed, the conditions became more difficult, and at 1st January the commission stopped working and I stopped heading the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I understand that. Was Dusko Tadic visiting Trnopolje camp with you whilst you were working with him on the commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time Dusko Tadic was not in the Trnopolje camp. He was on the commission with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all I ask, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I have a moment, your Honour? No, nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Witness, were there any records kept of the time, the times, rather, I suppose, each day when you were engaged on work of the commission, written records?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a written record at the Prijedor municipality, except that I did not have the possibility -- I did not see that decision. There is an official decision saying that I am the head of the commission, what am I supposed to do, what is my assignment and things like that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: No, I do not mean that, but were there daily records kept of the hours when you and your two other members of the commission were out in the field doing the work you have described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officially, no, but I kept my own record book, that is, I had my log book and then I noted that down, but had somebody -- did somebody else have such a record, no. It was simply a question of trust; that the commission would pick out the time which was most suitable. Whether we would work for three hours or for five hours or 10 hours, it depended on various things. It could depend on the head of the commission. In this particular case, it depended on me really, whether I would go out at 7 o'clock in the morning and stay until there was daylight. It really depended on a number of objective and subjective things and on the men who headed the commission, at least that is the tradition in that area, that a man who is put in charge of something is really responsible and he decides about these things, whether we would stay out for longer, for longer hours or whether we would work shorter hours but harder. It really depended on whether a car was available, on my free time, on weather conditions and so on and so forth. Sometimes we went out later and returned later, sometimes we went out earlier and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What I am concerned with is whether you have still in your possession your log book, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to look for it. I do have it. I do have it somewhere. When I was about to leave to come here, I tried to find it and I did not. After all, it was 1992. I am really sorry but I must have it somewhere. It was my personal diary. So that I will have to continue looking for it and I will try to send it to show you that we really went out into the field, at what time we set out and at what time we returned, if there was something specific which I noted down just for my own sake. I have been a field worker for ages and I always kept a kind of diary, and I do not remember names of people, but I do remember other things. I am not going to say that I am a good agronomist, but I think I am fairly knowledgeable about that particular area of work.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The next question I wanted to ask you was, do you know whether there would have been a record kept somewhere of the use of this car when it was driven by the driver? Would he keep a record and would that be maintained in some central office in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Professional municipal drivers, they must have their travel order and they must, of course, note down when they set out into the field, when they returned and, of course, their fuel consumption. I do not have this, but these records can be traced because the drivers, they of course have to do that because they are official cars, official vehicles or, rather, municipal, so they have to put it down, the time they leave, the time of departure, the time of return and things of that, the fuel and everything else, except that we since if we used private cars, then of course we did not do that or we did it for our own sake. But when I used the official vehicle of the agricultural station, then of course I needed a travel order always, time of departure, time of return, fuel consumption and everything else. You had to put it down to justify your costs and all these things.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Those records would still be maintained somewhere in the opstina I suppose, would they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, oh, yes, one would be able to trace them. It must be in existence somewhere because it is not -- it was not so long ago, and so these documents are kept for 10 years at least under our old laws. I do not know how it is now.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The next question on a quite different topic: when Mr. Tadic accompanied you, as a member of the commission, on these journeys, what was he wearing? Was he wearing a uniform or was he wearing ordinary civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic did not ask for me to be appointed to the commission. The commission was appointed by the Executive Board of the municipality ----

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: No, you misunderstand my question. I am simply asking, when he did accompany you what clothes did he wear? Did he wear a uniform or did he wear civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We all wore or, rather, tried to wear uniforms because it was safer for field work. I was also in a uniform. It was also fashionable in a way, whoever could lay his hands on a uniform. I mean, he felt and was more privileged, but I know that my uniform was poorer and Tadic's was better. But, in any event, I was not particularly keen on uniform, but I still wanted to have it because the situation was really not under control. It was easier to approach people or talk to people. When you would be in civilian clothes, then it could appear as if you were looking for something again privately for your own sake and, therefore, it was better. So I tried to combine things. I could not really lay my hands on a whole uniform, but I tried to combine. I did not have footwear which belonged to it, but our geodesic, she did not have uniform, she had civilian clothes, and Tadic and I were in uniforms and it was really advisable.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you remember what sort of uniform Mr. Tadic wore? We have heard of camouflage uniforms, we have heard of SMB uniforms. Which was he wearing or did he wear different uniforms at different times, and police uniforms also we have heard of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, as far as I can remember, Mr. Tadic had a multi-coloured, what we called a camouflage uniform, not the SMB of the old Yugoslavia. Those were worn by ordinary soldiers, by simple soldiers, who had no money to buy something else, a camouflage uniform. But we tried to somehow come by those new uniforms to look slightly better, to look like civilised soldiers, or whichever way you care to put it, although it was difficult to be that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just a few questions. What colour was the camouflage uniform? Is it a multi-colour, brown, green, light brown, dark brown, coffee colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, I am slightly handicapped. I really do not recall colours when they are not in front of my eyes. I know it was many colours, whichever colours were worn at the time. I really could not -- I am simply unable to describe what colour a person was wearing at a particular time. I never can do that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: That is OK. If homes were taken from individuals in Kozarac, taken from them, prior to October 1st 1992, I gather your commission would not have been involved in that because the commission did not exist, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tadic told me (and I was also aware of the fact) that there had been two commissions before me whose assignment was also to survey all this property which we then started doing, but of course they failed. When our commission was established, we knew that we would succeed because the three men appointed to it were all very serious, very thorough and we would really do good work, and Mr. Tadic when we met, because he also did not know me really, he said: "I will congratulate you if you succeed" and I told him: "Just you listen what this seasoned man will tell you and we shall succeed certainly", because one has to know how to work in a village. You have to know how to approach a villager, and if you have shown him that you are honest, that you are decent, then you cannot fail, and there is no distinction between rich and poor. You have to know how to approach it, and I have been working with villagers for years. So I knew how to approach a man, how to talk to people, how serious, what kind of a language, when to accept a cup of coffee from him or when not to accept it and that was my personal experience. For instance, I never allowed the commission to accept a cup of coffee in a house because then it would meaning sitting down and that would be that. So I never allowed such -- these kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know what commissions Mr. Tadic was talking about, the two commissions that existed before October 1st, for the reassignment or whatever of houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were similar to ours, except that they had no agronomists on these commissions. They were commissions which were composed of inexperienced people, mostly young, some girls who were either lawyers or, for instance, geodesics, surveyors. But they simply were not up to the task. I never really went into it. I did not want to. I did not particularly care to learn who were people were on these commissions. But, as far as I know, they were all rather inexperienced and that is why they did not succeed in completing the business.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know why Mr. Tadic was assigned to this commission? You have testified about your long and good experience. Was the other member of the commission a woman, but a woman who had this agronomist experience? If not agronomist, it was -- what was the experience of the other member of the commission, the woman? She was not a lawyer, I gather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was, no, she was not a lawyer. She was not a lawyer. She was a land surveyor. She carried those cadastral instruments and worked for the cadastral office, for the cadastre. She could identify every house. She knew owners because she had those cadastre books. She was a very serious professional. She knew how to take, where to take us. She knew where everything was and that is this field experience which is of tremendous importance when you go out into the field. When you have a dilettante who does not know anything, who does not know whose house is where, what is the cadastral municipality -- the cadastral area or the books or who is the owner of a particular house, and she had that kind of experience. She knew that. This little Gordana Sobot whom we called "Goca". She has been with the cadastre office for some 20 years.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Tadic had any prior experience in this type of work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not tell you that, but at that time since it was being done at the Local Commune where Mr. Tadic was in a way the head of that Local Commune, that is, I think, how he came to be appointed to the commission because it was his Local Commune. Whether he had any kind of experience in this kind of work, I really could not tell you. He was a third member of the commission, and the two of us were the main members. We were the ones who conducted the whole business, but it was simply to have a local person because we were working in that area so we needed a person from that area to be with us.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you make an estimate as to how many homes you handled, that is, how many homes were transferred, if I may use that expression? I just do not know what other expression to use, but how many homes were given to families or individuals by the Republika Srspka by your commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time while we still worked, over 90 houses had already been surveyed and were being moved -- and some of them were being moved in, because as we went over them and we were -- at my initiative, we would start one day from one end and the next day from the other, because there were people who were trying to misappropriate these things. There were some tractors transporting furniture. There were all sorts of things. I mean, the people really thought that they could take away things that were not theirs because the situation was so chaotic. So we thought -- I thought it would be better if we always started from a different part of the area, from either [redacted] or Kozarac or something. But I think that about 90 per cent were by that time issued these decisions and could move in and for others the decisions were pending. I know that many people were satisfied with the work of the commission because we had done a good job of work in some 10 or 15 days already. So that protocols were made and so that decisions were beginning to be issued, and what they would be given for use, what they had to look after, because if they were to move out of that particular house after three or six months, they also had to have an inspection to see whether the house was as it was when they had moved in. I believe that had we had another month at our disposable that the situation would have been quite clear but, unfortunately, the weather conditions were such that we had to interrupt. But, as far as I can remember, it was more than 150 houses that we surveyed during that time. As I said, I cannot find the diary, that log book, that I had there. I had the exact number. Whether it was 170 or 155, I do not know, but it must have been over 150 homes. Over 90, as we were going on with our work, 90 of those were already being moved in, that is, decisions had been issued for them.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So you surveyed 150, approximately, and of the 150, 90 had already been surveyed and approved as being subject to occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 90, yes, about 90, yes, had already been distributed.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So am I correct then that it was 60, approximately, houses that you surveyed and of that number you determined, well, you surveyed 150 but 90 of them had already been surveyed, but you did beginning work on the remaining and then made a decision as to whether they were habitable and then subject to being assigned to someone, is that correct? Is that the number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope you understand me about the 150 houses we surveyed, and some of these 150 had been settled on the basis of our own protocols, of the protocols issued by my commission. So between 90 and 150, some 60 houses had no documents yet. Later, these were also given special approvals for settlement for some people. But when that was done, how it was done, to whom it was given, I do not know. After 1st January 1993, I had nothing to do with any of such commissions so I cannot tell you what happened later and I was too busy at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Who made the decision then to make the actual assignment after you made a determination of suitability?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a central commission of the cadastral property service and they were the ones who were entitled, who were authorised, who had the criteria, as to the distribution and allocation of these houses. This was not part of our brief. Whatever we did would be nothing. It would be not legally valid. We could only provide protocols of the suitability and habitability, but they decided whether this, that or the other person would be given that house because they were empowered to do that by the Assembly of the municipality of Prijedor. They had a special rubber stamp and that was the central commission for the whole of the municipality; so to get that was a legal document really.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So that was the group you testified about yesterday, they made the final decision, is that correct? I think you testified yesterday that it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, right, right.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What was the name of that organisation, do you know, or the authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the cadastral property ownership service for the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You then would not know who was actually given the houses that you surveyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my area, some 90 per cent of the houses were given to refugees from Cazin, Krupa, from Bihac, Bugojno, Travnik, mostly refugees, because when I was thinking professionally this was good land, good for intensive farming and these people, in fact, needed my help, professional help, because they came from higher altitudes, used to different kinds of farming. So they would have to learn to farm in this new area with new kinds of products, produce, and in fact that is how I viewed the whole situation. That is why I professionally and privately was interested in who was getting this, not the names, but all kinds of people were settling there. In 90 per cent of those new settlers came from these places that I mentioned. Many of them are still there now and they do have a problem to adjust to new technology, to a new climate, to new sort of soil, because they were used to be working and living at altitudes of 1500 metres, while we are now talking about the altitude of 200 metres. So there are different varieties, different kinds of plants grow there, and this is my own observation now that these people need a lot of help.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know how many of those people were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean those who settled, who are settled there?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those who were given these houses, the use of the houses? I know that there are many mixed marriages, but not Muslims as such, those who have been coming from Cazin, but I know there were some members who were Muslim perhaps in mixed marriages. Maybe a husband was a Muslim or the wife was -- the wife Serb and so on. There were some mixed marriages. Two cases, I know, two Muslims had Serbian wives, for instance. They themselves served in the army of Republika Srpska and so they came to live there. These are the two cases I know, but there are many other mixed marriages, people coming from the regions that I described earlier and settled here in Kozarac -- in and around Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: One final question: you testified you felt that Mr. Tadic had every reason to have extremist views. What did you mean by that? You said he never expressed any extremist views to you, but he had every reason to have them. Why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, since following the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, within a month and a half following that recognition, the times were very difficult, very hard. There was a lot of intolerance, hatred, something that one can hardly imagine could happen. I do not know what their behaviour was like, and what happened during the clashes in and around Kozarac. I thought that he must have felt the tension. Although I know that people in Kozarac lived together in peace and quiet, I would be coming earlier to Kozarac, to Omarska and so on, and I would be eating, drinking with them, socialising with them and they were living together. But within a month and a half after the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it became quite tense. People were insulting each other. There were many abnormal forms of behaviour, insulting each other, as I said earlier. You could not even go into a pub or a cafe because you never knew who would tell you what and say to you what. So that is what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Nothing arises, your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Dasic, would you continue to look for those records, please, and if you are able to find them would you please provide them to Mr. Wladimiroff so that he can provide them to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will. I promise that I will do my best to try to find my diary and send it to you. These are my private documents. You will return them to me, of course? There is nothing there that could be used against me.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, and that really was not our intent. I accept what you say about the hours. I have no reason not to accept what you said personally. One final question: what kind of car was the official car that you used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a Golf, a Lada and Renault 4 and Stojadin, the Yugoslav make car. We had four different types of cars there. My company had a Stojadin and Renault 4 and the municipality had a Golf and Lada. These were the four kinds of cars that we used for our field trips. I told you that I use also the car from my own company for that purpose occasionally, while the municipality had a Golf and a Lada. In my company, we had a Stojadin which was Zastava 101 and Renault 4. So we had four kinds of cars that we used for our field trips.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I was just on my feet to tell you that we already asked for that log book.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I got the impression you did because he said he had tried to look for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right. So far he was not successful, but we will assist him to look for it again. We checked with the municipality for all the records, but we were not successful. We did exactly the same for what Judge Stephen was asking for.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you. Mr. Tieger, additional questions? No. Is there any objection then to Mr. Dasic being permanently excused, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, there is.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Dasic, you should make yourself available. You are free to go home, but you may be recalled as a witness before the Tribunal. So keep in touch with Mr. Wladimiroff and if you are recalled, then we will ask that you come again. Will you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There will be no problem. I will do my best ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- I will do everything.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you and thank you for listening to me.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff or Mr. Kay, would you call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was Nada Vlacina who was to be recalled for Mr. Tieger to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The usher realises that he should bring in Mrs. Vlacina? MRS. NADA VLACINA, recalled.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, Defence Exhibit 68A has not been admitted. Did you intend to offer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour. We are not going to tender it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Defence 61 which was the video that was taken of certain areas of Trnopolje some days ago. It was used and that has not been admitted. Did you intend to offer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, we want to tender that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to the video, if you remember? You can think about it and tell us after the recess, please. We will finish with Mrs. Vlacina. Mrs. Vlacina, you understand that you are still under oath, the oath that you took yesterday, to tell the truth? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vlacina, yesterday we briefly discussed your husband's occupation. You indicated that he stopped working just before the war. When the war began, your husband became part of the Serbian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first working day was Friday, 22nd May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He was a tank Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I do not know. My husband had some health problems before that, and during the whole of this time he was in Prijedor and only in 1994, in April, he was taken to the front. Before that he had to be in Prijedor and was under work obligation. That was, that was from April '92 -- from April '93 to April '94.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Initially, however, he was involved in the conflict in Kozarac, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you do not know ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he was at home. Every day and every night he spent at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You do not know where he was stationed during the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the witness just said that her husband was at home every day and every night he spent at home which rather implies ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am somewhat confused about the testimony, the dates, etc. But ask the question again, Mr. Tieger, without characterising her prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After your husband began serving on Friday, did he simply remain at home or did he have duties during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Friday? Which Friday do you mean? What kind of -- you mean on his job or in his company?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did your husband begin serving with the Serbian Army on Friday, May 22nd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. On Friday, 22nd May, he was on his job and around 4 o'clock he called me by a phone. He did not have the telephone. He called our neighbours and he said: "Do not worry, the roads are blocked. We cannot go via Kozarac, so I will take some side roads, take a bus and come home a bit later". So he came home around 5 o'clock, I think, half past 5. So on that day he was on his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At some point did he begin serving with the Serbian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When did he first begin serving with the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officially in April '94, because that was the time when he was mobilized. He put on the uniform and went to the battle front in Gradacac. You see, when the war came, when it started in Croatia, my husband did not go to the battle front in Croatia, and after that he had some health problems, very serious problems, nervous problems. He was in hospital and all military medical commissions gave him a temporary release from the army. He was not called to serve in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Until April '94?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, right. In April '94 he was truly mobilized. He put on the uniform, and went to Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There are some matters arising, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was 22nd May 1992 your husband's first or last working day at his company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 22nd May 1992 was Friday, the last day of my husband's work on his job in his company. The first working day was April when he was obliged to work, that was April '93, April '93, when he started working again. For a year until the end of April or 26th or 27th April 1994 he was mobilized. He received his summons. He was given the uniform and he left on that same day for Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Has your husband ever told you whether he has driven a tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is all I ask.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour, nothing further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I may be the only one who is having difficulty with the dates. Let me ask you just a couple of questions, Mrs. Vlacina. If I understand your testimony correctly, your husband's last working day was May 22nd 1992, is that correct, and that was with his company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Then he started working again with his company, the same company or a different company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same company, the same company. They called him back to work in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you testify that he was mobilized in 1993 but did not actually serve until April '94? That is when I am confused. When was he mobilized?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1994, also April, late April. He was given the summons. He was summoned to the army. He put on the uniform and went straight to the battle front, because following the events in Croatia my husband was in hospital in Banja Luka for a long time, and all the various medical, military medical committees declared him unfit to serve in the army. He was sent home for treatment and convalescence.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So he did not work at all between April 22nd 1992 and April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not work and even now he does not work.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour -- excuse me -- I think the Court meant May 22nd, if you wanted to check the transcript on that?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. May 22nd was the last working day, so that between that date and April 1993 your husband did not work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. He did not, and nobody ever called him to go to work.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And did not serve in the army during that period of time between May 22nd 1992 and April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between May 22nd?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: 1992, his last working day, and April 1993 when he started to work again, did he serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was called for the technical part, for maintenance and repairs, but he was not obliged to go every day. I cannot tell you in any more detail really.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know where he went and what kind of repairs he made on what kind of equipment? Do you know anything about what he was doing during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were technical interventions, I would say. This was only when he was needed.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know what he did when he left because he was needed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know where he went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was all in Prijedor, everything happened in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was he called by the Yugoslav National Army during this period between May 22nd 1992 and April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the army?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. He was working in the central workshop in Prijedor, but I do not know many more and I cannot answer your question.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So you do not know whether he was in the army during that period of time, is that what you are saying? Did he wear a uniform when he left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, everybody had to have a uniform. For me, officially, he left -- he went into the army in 1994 because that is when he put on the uniform and left.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he wear a uniform when he would leave to go to work on the technical equipment between May 22nd 1992 and April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was it a grey uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the SMB uniform. Everybody had that kind of uniform because the work obligation actually meant that they would be dressed like that and they would be called to do work.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, there are, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have referred to military service as well as work obligation. Were they two different things during this period in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how to answer this question because when the war broke out many people were mobilized and they left home and they would be away for 10 days, 20 days, a month. Those who had work obligation, they were mostly at home. They remained in Prijedor and they would be working seven to eight hours a day. So everybody who was truly mobilized, who were summoned into the army, they would go to the front, to break the corridor and so on, and so the troops left from Prijedor. I do not know for sure, because everybody had to come to a central collection point in Prijedor and then they would leave Prijedor and go somewhere. While people who had work obligations, they remained there and they had their normal working hours, five, six, seven, eight hours a day. But practically everybody was uniformed -- everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When your husband was called for technical assistance in Prijedor, was that work obligation or military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I honestly do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But was your husband mobilized at this time after 22nd May 1992 at any stage during that year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did he get summons and so on? He did not go -- he did not go to the battle front. He did not go anywhere. You mean whether he got official summons? I only know the unofficial summons in April 1994 when I saw him out of the house and when he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know how many times he assisted on technical matters in Prijedor and whilst he was at home in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every Saturday and Sunday he was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour, nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does that mean that Monday through Friday he would leave to assist on the technical matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what the role was. Everybody was doing something.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I am not asking what his role was. I am asking -- the question that Mr. Kay asked you was ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1992, you are asking?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The question that he asked you was, when did he go and your answer was, “when did he go... matters? Your answer was that he was home every Saturday and Sunday. That is not truly responsive unless I can assume that you meant, therefore, that he went to work on these technical matters Monday through Friday. That is what I assumed, but I thought it would be best to ask you that. So did he leave to work on these technical ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he worked, he worked and he would be coming back home at around 3 o'clock and was home every evening.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So he worked Monday through Friday on these technical matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do not know whether it was every day. It may not have been every day.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Maybe not every day, OK, but he was certainly at home ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I am quite sure, that every afternoon, every evening, every night he was home.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: That is what you remember, I am sure, but he was paid, was he not, because your apartment had been given to you by his previous employer, but he was not longer working, I gather, for this employer, so did you then have to pay rent -- I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was your apartment not given to you by his employer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did get the flat from the company, but when the war started nobody received any salary. There was no -- nothing was being paid. The mine company was not paying any wages or salaries. Only once they paid it in, I think it was in June or July, but for the rest of time my husband got no salary.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Nothing. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mrs. Vlacina being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, the same situation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Mrs. Vlacina, you are free to leave now but you should remain available to the Tribunal because you may be recalled as a witness. Keep in touch with Mr. Kay. If he indicates that you are to return, then you should return for testimony. Will you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Thank you very much for coming. We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay, would you call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, the next witness, your Honour, is to be known as Witness Y and will be giving his evidence under that pseudonym. Although it will be in open session for most of his evidence, part of it will have to be in closed session and he will have a facially distorted image for the passage that is in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Niemann, did you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is only, your Honour, I was responding to what happened just before the adjournment when you asked me about Exhibit 61D.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry, yes. I forgot about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Our position is, your Honour, we do not have any objection to its tender, but I do not think we have seen it all yet. My understanding is that only part of it has been played, but I might be wrong in that; if that is not the case, then perhaps all of it should be. The only matter is that we ask if the Defence could indicate (and it can be done from the Bar table) when the video was actually taken, at what time of the year and the date.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, have we seen the complete of 61?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we did was we had a tape and took out segments and we played three segments before that particular witness which we then made the Exhibit rather than the whole tape. The film itself was shot in August of this year by Mr. Wladimiroff ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is what I really wanted to ask!

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Hence the slight lurch to the left as he was walking!

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is OK. I had difficulty looking at the same time and pressing it. It is very difficult. OK, so what we have then is a video of a longer duration, but only certain clips of it were offered. Do you want to see the entire video before making ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. If that is all the Defence wish it to be as an Exhibit ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that all that is in?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- then there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is right. We filmed every house on that road. When it became clear we were not dealing with those, we took them out of the ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I see. 61B then will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You will call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Witness Y, please. WITNESS Y, called

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please take the oath that is being given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Witness Y, I would like you to look at this piece of paper and identify whether that is your proper name and once you have looked at it if it would be handed to the Prosecution and then to the Registry? Is that your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is my first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You will be known in court as "Witness Y". Can you confirm that you live in the area of Kozarac at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, do you want me to say the number of the house, the street and all the rest? I live in ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, I am going to stop you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all we need. When did you move to that area of Kozarac? How long have you lived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I moved into the area of Kozarac on 2nd August '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where had you lived before 2nd August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in Gradina which is the municipality of Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For how long have you lived in municipality of Velika Kladusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the municipality of Velika Kladusa, I was born on 2nd January '64 and I lived in that village until the primary school. Since primary school, I went to Bihac. That is where I completed secondary school and High School. After the completion of that, I found a job at Glina where I built a house and I worked there for a year until the war broke out in Croatia. After the beginning of war in '91, that was, I again lived in that village until I left in '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was your occupation in 1991? What was your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a mechanical engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You referred to going to school and your education. Were you qualified as an engineer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a high mechanical school, that is, I am -- was a shop floor engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were living in Velika Kladusa were you living with your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I lived my father, mother, sister, grandfather, grandmother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you married?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I married in '91.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have a child?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a child in Kozarac. He was born on 13th November '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why did you move to Kozarac on 2nd August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we moved because we could not live there, we could not survive there. I am talking in my own name, my house burnt down sometime in July. I cannot remember exactly. It was before August, towards the end of July. My father's house and his land and everything was burnt down. So it was simply not safe there and, therefore, we had to leave what we had and go, go anywhere just to save our lives and survive. That was our only objective, to live and survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that an Orthodox religion as well that you follow, the Orthodox religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The other members of your family, you told us about your mother and father, were they Serbs as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your wife to whom you are married, was she a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She is also a Serb, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did the house where you lived come to be burnt down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we, when was that -- when did this thing start in Bosnia, sometime since April or May, and up there we were adjacent to the municipality of Glina and the municipality of Dvor, and we had very many relatives up there, and we escaped, that is, we took out something that we thought was valuable, that is, some cattle and vehicles, tractors, and we took them up there and we were up there for about two months. We managed somehow to survive there for about two months until July, and then we had to abandon it all and leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the dominant ethnic population in that area where you were living in Velika Kladusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the municipality or my village?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, tell us about the municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see, municipality. I think, well, at that time I did not really, I was not interested in this, that is before the war, I did not care about it that much, but I think that there were about three or four per cent of the population of Serb origin in that municipality, I should say that, but as regards the municipality we had a larger area, that is, we had a lot of land. I think that about 33 per cent of the area of Kladusa was Serb property and the rest is where Muslims lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your village in that area that you have told us about, what was the dominant ethnic population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not many. In my village, specifically -- for instance, in my village of Gradina there were about 70, 70 households, and it was by and large a Serb village. The population there was largely Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were other houses burnt down belonging to Serb people in that village where you lived or was it just your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite a number of houses burned down. All those houses closer, closer to the Muslims, they all burned down. A number of houses burned down and when we were leaving some were still standing, but they were burned down later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did they come to be burnt down? What was happening in the area that caused them to be damaged or destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not really understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If they burnt down, who set fire to them or what happened to them? How did they get on fire if they burnt down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was this way, because of that, towards the end of July, we had to leave.
