I was simply too busy elsewhere, and I joined the SDS so that I could help the population which had moved there in the first place, to have a contact with Prijedor because somebody had to represent that population or ask something on behalf of that population in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: MR. DUSAN VAJAGIC, recalled. Examined by MR. KAY, continued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vajagic, you had dealings with Mr. Tadic as Secretary of the local SDS as well as through his involvement in the Local Commune. How did he spend his time? What work was he doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the meetings of the local committee of the SDS of Kozarac, and there were about 12 to 15 members of the local committee, I do not know the exact number but, anyway, at these meetings we would agree as to what needed to be done. This was some kind of preparation for work and you assign, make assignments, assign duties for different people for different things. Since Dusko Tadic was the Secretary of the local community and President of the SDS, his duties were most numerous. Everything revolved around him. The whole organisation of work went through his desk, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he work hard at this job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So did he spend any time actually making these ideas and policies and decisions work? Did he himself get involved in helping to rebuild the local community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the meetings of the local committee we would agree as to what needed to be done. We would divide, distribute, the duties, assignments, and usually most of the assignments went to Dusko Tadic especially when something needed to be done in the municipal town hall, in the power utility, the postal service, the veterinary station, the schools, so that we could organise repairs of our school and so on. Most of these contacts had, in fact, been allotted to Dusko Tadic as the Secretary of the local committee and local community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For how long were you Secretary of the local Kozarac SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was Secretary, I do not know exactly how long. I forget the dates now when I started on that post and then when I ended, so I cannot answer very precisely, but I was in that position in 1993, the whole of 1993, and part of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In 1992, from your dealings with Dusko Tadic, could you tell if he was involved in Trnopolje camp in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did any of the work that you and he and others were involved in also require you to do any work in or around Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We had nothing to do and we had no contact with that part of the country, with Trnopolje, which had a collection centre, because that part belonged to another Local Commune and we had no authority and no jurisdiction, so to speak, over that part of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to describe the character of Dusko Tadic from your dealings with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly, I do not know how to put it, I did not have the -- I did have the impression of a man who is a family man, a man who was willing and eager to help the people, so he was a good man trying to help. I never had an opportunity to notice him involved in any kinds of clashes or conflicts with people or quarrel. He was not a quarrelling person at all. He was not a drinker, as far as I know. So that is what I could tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage we ask that the Court go into closed session to deal with a matter that the Court ruled upon earlier today and we know that this witness will be able to assist. I have spoken to Mr. Niemann about it during the short adjournment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will need five minutes and we will then return and we will be in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. MR. DUSAN VAJAGIC, continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell me your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 19th November 1956.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was your father's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milos.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your evidence that you approached the accommodation commission for a house when you first arrived in the opstina Prijedor, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the commission had made a list, a survey of houses before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. You do not know when that list had been compiled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not long before our arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you then consulted this list, did you, when you arrived in the Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not see the list. I was simply told that I was to be accommodated in that particular house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A man who was on the commission, who was responsible for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the accommodation commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of the commission which had took stock of which, had taken stock of the houses available and those families which were arriving. They also had a list of families which were arriving, and they followed the list down and they had the list of houses and on the basis of that they allocated houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the name of the man that was on the commission that told you what particular house you were to have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a man from my village, from my native village, from Gradina, because we had three men whom we assigned on Banja before we left, three men who were sent to Prijedor and worked with the commission appointed by the municipality of Prijedor to do precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know all three members of the commission, from Gradina, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: OK. Can you tell me the names of all three members that you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. They were [redacted], Nikola Guglata, and Dusan Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Which one did you approach or which one told you that you could have the house that you moved into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Dusan Mitrovic who told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from these three members that were on the accommodation commission, were there any people from the local area of Prijedor, Kozarac in particular, who were represented on this commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard from us that there was a three-member commission from Prijedor, but I do not know the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You do not know their names. When you were allocated this house were you given a key or a titled document or some sort of written authority or just told to turn up there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived in Kozarac on 2nd August I was told, I was shown that I was to move into that house without any papers or keys. One did not need the key because the house was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who showed you the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusan Mitrovic, the member of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This house had belonged to a Muslim family previously, had it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess so, most probably, because I do not know. I did not live there before, so ....

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you were given no paper. Did you have to sign any documents to say that you were taking over this house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You did not have to pay anything at all, I take it, when you took over the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you find any furniture or other documents in the house when you moved into it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was furniture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That furniture obviously did not belong to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it did not belong to me, but I found it, I mean, it was in the house when I entered and I went on using it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you been to this area in Kozarac before August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the ratio or the proportions of Serb people in the area of Kozarac to other nationalities such as Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in the area of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In Kozarac, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There was obviously previously many more Muslims, was there not, than Serbs by the number of available houses in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just from common sense and general observations you could have concluded that because of the available accommodation that was there, that prior to 1992 in the Kozarac region the Serbian people would have been in the minority, that is right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic was an extremely important man in the local area, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a man in the Local Commune. He was also on the SDS, but when we had already settled in, later on. I do not know what happened before I arrived, but when I met him he was already discharging those duties that I spoke about earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the local area of Kozarac he was the most important man, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In your evidence-in-chief you described him as being a person, all the business, all the affairs which concerned the organisation of life in the area, all this done by the Secretary of the Local Commune. Now someone responsible and concerned for the organisation of life in the area would be extremely important, would he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he worked but other people helped him. He was not all by himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But he was the first among the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, and I think you go on a little further in your evidence-in-chief to describe him in his capacity as President of the SDS, that everything revolved around him, that is the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, by and large all the meetings that were organised were convened by him as President, and assignments were allocated at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say that you later joined the SDS party and indeed became the secretary of the party in the local area, secretary of the SDS, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at a meeting of the local board, simply those people on the local board as they were mostly farmers, there were very few people with some education and that is how they nominated me as a secretary and others accepted and that is how I became the secretary of the local SDS board in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That was a very important position too, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, had circumstances been normal, then perhaps you could have said, you could say that because there was this vacancy which had to be filled, but because of some other things, because of other reasons, it was not all that important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was the only party that was operational in the area, was it not, at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What I mean to say is in Kozarac you did not have in the local school a meeting of the SDS and in the Post Office a meeting of the HDZ, and in some other location a meeting of the SDA going on all at the same time, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not -- I fail to understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry. I will not press it. In order to achieve things throughout the opstina of Prijedor, the approval of the SDS was necessary, was it not? It was the controlling political party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a political party, but as far as I know at that time we all acted in a similar way, both those who were involved in party activity and those who were not members of the party, so as to organise their life in Kozarac, simply to survive there. We came, we had fled from other areas, and we had had to live somewhere, we had to organise ourselves somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But being at that time in 1992, in the fall of 1992 being a member of the SDA would not have been terribly influential, would it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You do not know. Did you meet the secretary of the SDA at any stage after you were made secretary of the SDS for the Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because there was no SDA in our territory at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is primarily because most of its members had been removed from the area, that is right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am really at a loss how to answer this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to Kozarac in August '92. I did not find Muslims there. I do not know when they left or how or whether there had been any other inhabitants there. I know what the situation was on 2nd August when I moved in. Whether there had been an SDA before that or not I would not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You knew that the SDS was primarily committed in terms of the its political philosophy to obtaining an area, a homeland, for the Serbian people, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wanted to provide freedom, a free life for its people. You can say some fatherland for its people where they could live.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That was its objective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That was the objective of the SDS party, was it not, to obtain a territory for the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could understand it and can understand it, not to obtain a territory, but to preserve life of people and the Serb people in that part, if you want to put it that way, or in Bosnia-Herzegovina at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Indeed to cleanse that territory of people who were not of the same Serbian nationality, that is right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not say that, nor did I understand it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You told us a moment ago that obviously there must have been a considerable Muslim population there and that when you arrived they were not there any more. You tell us you do not know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if it was large. Probably it was, but I do not know because I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, the people, the Muslim people that were there were not there when you arrived. They had left, had they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You knew that clearing the land of the Muslim people was an objective of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was not the objective, and I left my home and my father's home. I had to live somewhere, so I came where I was offered, where I could live and organise my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You came to an area that had been cleansed under the authority and auspices of the SDS, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, when you arrived at that place, so far as you knew, it could well be a Muslim stronghold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not there at the time and I do not know what could have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am saying when you came, at the time that you came in August of 1992, you knew that it was controlled by the Serbs and that it had been cleansed of Muslims, you knew that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew that the area was under Serb control, but whether it had been cleansed, we did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say it was under Serb control, politically it was under the control of the SDS, that is right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In all likelihood, but at that time I was not a member of the SDS yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you then did become the secretary for the local area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this stage, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing at this stage, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Witness, a couple of questions I wanted to ask you. The first one was, when you saw Mr. Tadic during the period that he was secretary of the SDS and you were working with him in Kozarac, was he wearing a uniform at all times or at no time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusan Tadic was the President of the local SDS board and not the secretary. In the beginning while he was on the Reserve Police Force he did have a uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What sort of uniform was that? What did it look like, just very roughly, what colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a conventional multi-coloured, camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Then later he ceased to wear a uniform and wore ordinary civilian clothes, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when he left the Reserve Police Force he wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: About when did that happen, can you put a month to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometime towards the end of October or in the early days of November '92. I do not remember exactly, but it was roughly about the time.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes. A quite different question. You succeeded Mr. Tadic in 1992 as secretary of the commune -- I am sorry, as secretary of the local branch of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Dusan Tadic was the President ----

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- of the board, as you put it, but he was the President of the local, the chairman of the local board of the SDS. When I joined it I became the secretary of the local board of the SDS and these are two different positions.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I follow. You then served with him on the board of the SDS, he as President and you as secretary, after you were appointed. Then at sometime he ceased to be President, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he ceased to being a President when he left Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes. About when was that, again just a month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was sometime in mid '93. I cannot be more exact, but it must be towards the middle of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you know why Mr. Tadic left Kozarac in, was it mid-1993? Do you know why he left Kozarac and where he went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing arises, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This witness will be recalled on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Sir, you are free to leave now, but you should return Tuesday -- how are we going to handle the order of witnesses on Tuesday? Well, you lawyers will work it out, but you are to return on Tuesday of next week to continue your testimony, sir. We are now adjourned until Tuesday at 11 a.m.
